Risk of Spread

WHO Rapid Risk Assessment

For the latest risk assessment, see the WHO Rapid Risk Assessment: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus (v4), 20 August 2026.

WHO’s overall risk and confidence ratings by geography:

GeographyOverall riskConfidence
Democratic Republic of the CongoVery HighModerate
Countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the CongoHighModerate
Rest of the African RegionLowModerate
GlobalLowHigh
At a glance

Nearby countries, particularly Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, face the highest near-term risk of imported Bundibugyo virus cases from the DRC. Rankings for more distant countries vary across analyses, driven by differences in how each model treats air travel, land travel, and the assumed spatial distribution of source cases. Evidence suggests that surveillance is best concentrated on the highest-probability importation routes. Confidence is moderate, with relative destination rankings holding up better across analyses than the absolute probabilities attached to them.

Synthesizing evidence¶

State of the evidence¶

As of 19 October 2026, WHO has reported 9,637 confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) across 66 health zones in eight provinces.[1] Sixteen analyses are included, the most recent with a snapshot date of 10 October 2026.[2] Eleven provide risk-of-spread estimates: nine address cross-border or international importation, and two address spread within DRC.[3][4] Some share authors and/or data sources, so they are not fully independent. For example, Klein et al. and Verheyden & Mudogo (2026b) both use Flowminder data.[5][6]

How the estimates compare¶

Analyses that rank countries by their likelihood of importing cases from the DRC outbreak largely agree on the highest-risk countries and diverge further down the list. Chamla et al. place Uganda (94.2%) and South Sudan (69.3%) far above DRC’s other neighboring countries,[7] Epistorm’s October update keeps that order, with Uganda carrying 98.0% of relative risk outside DRC and South Sudan 53.5% of the remainder once Uganda is set aside,[8][9] and Fanelli et al. (2026a) rank South Sudan at highest importation risk.[10] Rwanda and Burundi are low in Chamla et al., but Fanelli et al. (2026a) rate them high and attribute the difference to spatial heterogeneity and conflict-adjusted travel times,[11] and Li et al. rate them very high, even above South Sudan.[12]

The main divergence is methodological. Air-traffic analyses elevate international hubs such as Belgium, France, South Africa, Kenya, and the UAE,[13] or France, Italy, and the UK within Europe,[14] while analyses combining land and air mobility place a largely contiguous belt of African countries at highest risk.[15] Assessments focused on North Africa and Europe rate introduction as very low to low,[16] and the US assessment rates overall risk to the US population as low, based on an extremely low likelihood of transmission.[17] Rankings hold across scenarios and assumptions even where absolute estimates do not.[18][19] From June to October the top tier holds while the list of higher-risk African countries lengthens, with Kenya, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, and Ethiopia following South Sudan in Epistorm’s October update,[9] but differing methods and time horizons make it unclear whether this reflects outbreak spread or re-estimation.

The importations into Kenya and Nigeria fall within the modeled higher-risk tiers.[15] As of 19 October, Kenya has confirmed nine cases, eight of them among relatives and hospital staff of the imported index case who were already in quarantine.[20] It ranks behind South Sudan in Epistorm’s October update and appears as a hub in air-based analyses.[9][13] The Nigeria case, a traveler from Uganda, was confirmed 13 days after symptom onset,[21] and Nigeria is one of three geographically distant countries in the Fanelli et al. (2026a) high-risk quartile.[15]

Within DRC, Okingo et al. separate importation from amplification risk. Health zones near the affected area rank high for introduction, while high potential for sustained transmission appears mainly in more distant urban centers, including Kinshasa.[22][23]

Key uncertainties and assumptions¶

Four assumptions recur across the analyses, and where scenarios were tested, rankings were more robust than absolute estimates.[18][19]

First, mobility inputs are a recurring source of uncertainty in the importation estimates. Land-border data are scarce,[24] and the Uganda district model uses a single 10-day window that may miss movements through unofficial crossings.[25] Fanelli et al. (2026a) assume infected people travel only during the latent phase, although some with early or mild symptoms may still travel.[26] Chamla et al. identify their travel-while-infectious parameters as the principal source of uncertainty,[27] and varying them moves South Sudan by about 20 percentage points but Uganda by under 5, because Uganda’s probability is already near the upper end of its range.[28]

Second, source-area incidence is uncertain. Reported counts mix transmission with expanded testing and reporting backlogs, so the rise in DRC counts cannot be read directly as acceleration.[29] Epistorm estimates that about 69% of symptomatic cases have been reported,[30] and Bouhentala & Kadir note that reporting dates in public aggregate data do not represent symptom onset.[31] Confirmed DRC cases have also risen roughly sixfold, from 1,561 on 4 July[32] to 9,637 on 19 October,[1] so estimates fitted to earlier counts, such as the 4 July cutoff in Fanelli et al. (2026a), predate most of this growth.

Third, importation estimates do not by themselves describe onward spread. Arrival probability measures importation, not onward spread.[33] Containment depends on surveillance, diagnostic capacity, workforce, and infection prevention and control.[34] Fanelli et al. (2026a) note that operational preparedness is not determined solely by structural readiness indicators.[35]

Fourth, some analyses do not model border or screening measures. Epistorm does not simulate entry screening or restrictions on travelers[36] and Kinoshita et al. do not account for enhanced screening,[37] so absolute risks in these analyses are probably overstated, with conditional rankings less affected.[38] Chamla et al. instead include point-of-entry detection sensitivity.[39]

Some analyses also rest on structural choices of their own. Kinoshita et al. borrow a hazard parameter from the 2013-2016 West African epidemic,[40] and Li et al. treat all cumulative cases as potentially infectious, a worst-case assumption.[41]

What would reduce uncertainty¶

First, outbreak-specific, repeated mobility data, including movements through unofficial crossings, would help most, since Chamla et al., Walekhwa et al., and Fanelli et al. (2026a) all name mobility gaps.[42][25][24] Flowminder, whose movement data are already used in several DRC analyses,[43][5][6] is one source of this kind of mobility data.

Second, case counts aggregated by date of report cannot be used to separate transmission from changing ascertainment,[44] and Bouhentala & Kadir could not estimate onset-to-isolation delays, serial intervals, or health-zone-specific growth from them.[45] Chamla et al. recommend that future iterations integrate line lists and contact-tracing data.[42]

Third, measures of operational readiness, rather than structural indicators alone, for top-ranked destinations would show how well each could contain an imported case, which importation rankings cannot.[34] Useful measures include laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, and contact tracing,[46] isolation capacity and sample transport,[47] and referral readiness,[48] since the size of an outbreak seeded by an importation depends on containment capacity as well as on the importation itself.[49][35]

Open questions¶

Several analyses call for iterative updating as data accrue,[50][51] including weekly model reruns based on the latest mobility and case data.[52] Whether travel by people with early or mild symptoms,[26] humanitarian, military, or charter flights,[53] or changing land mobility[25] would materially shift rankings remains unresolved. Walekhwa et al. also call for outbreak-specific estimates of BDBV biological parameters, particularly the infectious period and serial interval.[54]

What this means for the response¶

based on current information, Uganda and South Sudan are among the countries most likely to experience case importations,[7][10] but importation risk and readiness to contain a case do not necessarily go together. South Sudan pairs high importation risk with documented gaps across all five WHO preparedness domains,[49] whereas Uganda’s repeated importations have not led to sustained community transmission.[55] In Kenya, eight of nine confirmed cases were already in quarantine when they developed symptoms.[20] Zambia, Ethiopia, and Tanzania combine high exposure with stronger capacity, while Burundi and the Central African Republic share South Sudan’s pairing of high importation risk and readiness gaps.[10] Fanelli et al. (2026a) likewise frame prioritizing surveillance and response as depending both on where imported infections are most likely to occur and on whether recipient countries are prepared to detect and contain them.[56]

For DRC, the evidence supports attention beyond the eastern hotspots, including Kinshasa and other urban health zones where amplification potential is high despite distance from the outbreak.[23] Klein et al. likewise find that allocation of diagnostic capacity cannot be based only on current confirmed cases, because the major value comes from stopping future lineages,[57] and Verheyden & Mudogo (2026b) caution that low observed local incidence should not be treated as zero risk where mobility and reporting gaps remain.[58] Spread into South Sudan, or amplification in Kampala, Kigali, or Kinshasa, would reshape exposure patterns, including importation pressure to Europe.[59][60]

For more distant African destinations, the Nigeria case, in which the patient first sought care at a private facility four days after symptom onset and was confirmed nine days later, illustrates why Bouhentala & Kadir identify early recognition in routine clinical care as the priority for preparedness.[21][61]

For destinations outside Africa, risk of introduction is assessed as low overall,[16][17] although France and Belgium rank high as arrival points in Kinoshita et al. and Li et al.[13][12] For North Africa and Europe, Bouhentala & Kadir recommend focused preparedness, including fully documented exposure histories, rapid isolation, validated diagnostics, protected clinical care, and contact management, rather than reliance on border screening,[62] whereas Li et al. say their high-risk countries, including France and Belgium, warrant enhanced entry screening.[12]

Epistorm (10 Oct 2026)
Ebola Bundibugyo Virus — DRC · Spread Risk Assessment #9 · Local Transmission Scenarios¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates transmission parameters, the current transmission level and the true burden of the outbreak in DRC, and projects its course to 30 November 2026.[63] It re-runs a metapopulation transmission model (GLEAM, with a care pathway from community to hospital to treatment centre) fitted to the rise in reported cases between 31 July and 30 September 2026.[64][65] It compares three scenarios in which 50%, 60% or 75% of symptomatic cases are isolated.[66] The 60% scenario is best supported, with the effective reproduction number close to 1 (0.95 in October).[67][68] That scenario projects 10,465 reported cases by 31 October.[69] International spread is out of scope.[70]

Estimate¶

Headline (60% isolation scenario, DRC nationally): The early-phase R₀ is 1.87 [1.69 – 2.09] and the doubling time is 13.2 [9.8 – 17.6] days.[71] About 69% [53 – 88] of all symptomatic cases since the start of the epidemic have been reported.[30] Rt was 0.98 in August and 0.95 in October.[68] The model gives 9,069 [8,531 – 9,727] reported cases on 10 October against 8,978 observed.[72] By 31 October it projects 15,225 [12,151 – 19,694] true symptomatic cases, of which 10,465 [9,433 – 11,835] are expected to be reported, with about 83 [47 – 150] new symptomatic cases per day.[73] By 30 November it projects 12,259 [10,446 – 15,059] reported cases, corresponding to about 17,741 true symptomatic cases.[74]

Range across isolation scenarios: R₀ rises from 1.71 [1.57 – 1.87] at 50% to 2.13 [1.88 – 2.36] at 75% isolation.[75] October Rt is 1.00 under 50%, 0.95 under 60% and 0.86 under 75%.[76] On 31 October, reported cumulative cases are 10,979 [9,786 – 12,219] (50%) and 9,859 [8,948 – 11,084] (75%), and true cumulative cases are 16,493 [12,781 – 24,114] (50%) and 12,941 [10,507 – 15,280] (75%).[77][78] On 30 November, reported cumulative cases are 13,382 [11,132 – 15,950] (50%) and 11,071 [9,528 – 13,442] (75%), and true cumulative cases are 19,728 [14,711 – 29,049] (50%) and 14,399 [11,174 – 18,147] (75%).[79][80] The scenarios differ more in true burden than in reported counts.[81] Reported cases per day stay roughly flat under 50% isolation (about 80 on 31 October and 80 on 30 November), decline slowly under 60% (64 and 56) and decline faster under 75% (47 and 34).[82]

Probabilities by 30 November: Reported cases are very likely to exceed 10,000 under 50% and 60% isolation (> 99% and 99%) and likely under 75% (82%), and exceeding 20,000 reported cases is very unlikely in all scenarios (< 1%).[83] The probability of 50 or more new cases per day is 94% under 50%, 79% under 60% and 36% under 75% isolation, and transmission is not expected to end by 30 November under any scenario.[84]

Methods¶

GLEAM care-pathway transmission model: GLEAM is an Africa-wide metapopulation network coupled by daily commuting matrices and origin-destination passenger flows from IATA and OAG.[85] Within each basin, a Legrand-like SEIHFR scheme represents community, health-facility-only and isolation pathways.[86] Transmission is overdispersed, with a small share of cases generating most secondary infections (dispersion k = 0.1).[87] A gradual isolation ramp of 1 percentage point per day starts after each area’s intervention trigger.[88] It produces reported and true case trajectories for DRC nationally, under 50%, 60% and 75% isolation.

Two-stage Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) calibration: Stage 1 selects trajectories consistent with early cross-border onsets in Uganda and early activity in Beni. Stage 2 fits the reported DRC counts.[89] The fit targets the increase in reported cases since 31 July, because earlier cases were partly added retrospectively.[90] Isolation scenarios are compared with Bayes factors.[91] The scenario ranking is the same for ABC tolerances between 3% and 10%.[92]

Effective reproduction number (Rt) estimation: Rt is the Cori estimator applied to simulated true daily onsets, with a 7-day sliding window and a gamma serial interval (mean 15.3 days, SD 9.3 days).[93] It is computed for DRC nationally.

Assumptions¶

Isolation level and ascertainment: Each scenario sets a target isolation level (50%, 60% or 75%).[94] Reporting is modelled as proportional to isolation, α(t) = c × Q(t), with every isolated case assumed reported and ascertainment capped at 1.[95] Projections assume each scenario’s isolation level is maintained and that ascertainment keeps tracking isolation.[96] Because the epidemic level before 31 July is only indirectly constrained, the overall ascertainment and true case numbers carry wide intervals.[97]

Isolation ramp timing: Each DRC basin starts a ramp of 1 percentage point per day when its cumulative onsets first reach 80. Bunia has a fixed start on 20 May 2026, and Uganda is held at 80% throughout.[98] Isolation and case-finding timings are applied homogeneously within each basin, although real-world coverage varies by location and over time.[99]

Reporting delay: Onset-to-report follows a gamma distribution with mean 5 days and SD 3.5 days, held constant over time.[100] SDs of 2.5 and 5 days give the same results.[101] Changes in the delay over time and batch updates of reported counts are not modelled.[102]

Transmissibility and natural history: Overdispersion k = 0.1 is assumed.[103] The baseline R₀ split is Community : HCF : Funeral at 0.44 : 0.22 : 0.34.[104] Residual nosocomial transmission in the isolation pathway is 10% of the routine HCF rate, an assumed value.[105] The latent period is U(5, 10) days.[106] The onset-to-admission time is 2 days on the isolation track.[107]

Seed and priors: The epidemic originates in Ituri with 5 infectious cases on the inferred start date.[108] The R₀ prior is U(1.2, 4.0) and the start-date prior is U(1 February, 15 March 2026).[109]

Mobility and interventions: Latent individuals are fully mobile, while 50% of symptomatic community cases remain mobile and isolated and hospitalised cases do not travel.[110] Mobility is held static, with no behavioural reduction, border closure or seasonality in transmissibility.[111] No vaccination is modelled.[112]

Calibration tolerance: Samples with distance ≤ 5% are accepted.[113] The scenario ranking is the same for tolerances between 3% and 10%.[92]

Limitations¶

Reporting-process simplifications: Reporting of new cases is assumed proportional to isolation with a constant factor per trajectory.[114] The onset-to-report delay is an assumption held constant, and changes in the delay over time and batch updates of reported counts are not modelled.[102]

Weak constraint on early epidemic size: The level of the epidemic before 31 July is only indirectly constrained, so overall ascertainment and the true number of cases carry wide intervals.[97] The early epidemic size is only loosely constrained.[115] Cases detected before and around the May alert were partly added retrospectively, so the cumulative level up to the first August report is not used as a fitting target.[90]

Hospital and isolation occupancy not compared: Model occupancy of the hospital and isolation compartments is not compared with the reported number of patients in isolation in this report, pending checks of the definition of the reported figure and treatment-centre length of stay.[116]

Homogeneity and static mobility: Isolation and case-finding timings are applied homogeneously within each basin; real-world coverage varies.[99] Mobility is held static, with no behavioural reduction, no border closure and no seasonality in transmissibility.[111]

Validation and precision: Projections are validated on a single held-out count (10 October).[117] Fewer simulations are accepted under 75% isolation, so its estimates are less precise.[118]

Trend interpretation: The data capture the slowdown itself, not yet its outcome.[119]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: DRC cumulative reported cases from 31 July to 30 September 2026 were used in the fit, and the 10 October count was held out.[120] The fit uses increments since 31 July at seven situation-report dates (+882, +1,701, +2,039, +2,576, +3,268, +4,099 and +4,626 cases).[121] The reported-count projection is anchored at 3,674 cases.[122] The 10 October count is 8,978.[123] The same situation reports give 4,336 cumulative deaths across 65 health zones, and 945 patients in isolation.[124] Stage 1 calibration uses 2–4 early cross-border onsets in Uganda and 2–80 early cumulative onsets in Beni.[125] Uganda’s 20 laboratory-confirmed cases (2 deaths) and one case in Kenya are mentioned as context.[126]

Auxiliary data: Mobility inputs are IATA Passenger Intelligence Services and OAG origin-destination passenger flows plus daily commuting matrices.[85] Dwell times and severity values come from the literature, including Wamala et al. for the 2007–2008 Uganda BVD outbreak.[127][128] Isolation-pathway case-finding timings follow the 2018 North Kivu RVEAP response.[129] The model structure follows the Legrand-type SEIHFR scheme.[130] The 5-day report delay is an assumption, described as a typical delay from onset to hospital or ETC admission.[131]

Epistorm (7 Oct 2026)
Ebola Bundibugyo Virus — DRC · Spread Risk Assessment · International Dissemination¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

The analysis does not estimate outbreak size. It describes where an exported case is most likely to be detected, given that at least one export occurs, rather than asserting that an export will occur.[132][133] It combines air-travel and short-scale commuting flows into a mobility-only relative importation risk over a two-week horizon.[134] Uganda alone carries 98.0 % of the non-DRC relative risk.[8] With Uganda removed, South Sudan leads the remaining international destinations with ~53 %, followed by Kenya (~12 %) and the Central African Republic (~7 %).[135] The absolute probability of any single international export remains small.[136]

Estimate¶

The analysis does not report an outbreak size estimate; it reports conditional relative importation risk. Across neighbouring countries, 99.0 % of the city-level relative risk sits in five cities: Kasese (UGA, 58.4 %), Pakuba (UGA, 28.6 %), Arua (UGA, 10.8 %), Juba (SSD, 0.9 %), and Rumbek (SSD, 0.15 %).[137] In the international tail, South Sudan takes 53.5 % (Juba 45.9 %, Rumbek 7.6 %), followed by Kenya (12.0 %), the Central African Republic (6.9 %), the UAE (3.2 %), Tanzania (2.9 %), and Ethiopia (1.7 %).[9] Africa retains 86.3 % of the tail, followed by Europe 5.2 %, the Middle East 4.8 %, Asia 2.6 %, and the Americas 0.9 %.[138] Beyond the UAE, intercontinental destinations sit at roughly 1 % or less.[139] These values are shares of export probability if an export occurs, not absolute probabilities of export.[140] No uncertainty intervals or scenario ranges are reported. The ranking applies to the two-week window from the 7 October 2026 snapshot.

Methods¶

Mobility-only relative importation risk (GLEAM-based): The approach follows the GLEAM (Global Epidemic and Mobility) computational framework.[141] For each destination, the model estimates the probability that an infected person from the affected area travels there, given at least one exported case, and outputs a relative risk distribution normalised to sum to one.[142] Inputs are IATA and OAG origin–destination air passenger flows plus short-scale commuting patterns between adjacent subpopulations.[143] No transmission model is used.[132] The framework is unchanged from earlier reports in the series (Reports #1 to #4 and #6).[134] The same underlying distribution is presented in two views: city-level risk across DRC’s neighbouring countries before renormalisation, and an international tail with only Uganda removed and the remainder renormalised over 120 destinations reachable by air.[144]

Assumptions¶

Conditional framing and horizon: Values are conditional on at least one international export occurring, and describe how export probability is distributed across destinations, not the absolute probability for any destination.[145] They describe where an exported case would likely land within the next two weeks.[146] For the tail, Uganda is removed and the remainder renormalised to sum to one.[147]

Incubation period: The incubation period of 2–21 days (average ~11 days) constrains the window within which an exported case could travel while infectious or pre-symptomatic.[148]

Traveller homogeneity: Sociodemographic attributes of travellers are not incorporated, and travel probability within a catchment is treated as independent of these attributes and of specific location within the catchment.[149] Estimates apply to general-population traffic and exclude repatriation flights, responder evacuations, and other ad-hoc operational movements.[150]

Independence of importations: Importations are modelled as statistically independent events, and a multi-case cluster travelling together counts as a single importation event.[151] The authors state the model may then under-count distinct exposure events while correctly counting distinct geographic seedings.[152]

No border-control measures: The model does not simulate entry screening, restrictions on travellers from the affected area, or air-service suspensions.[36] Such measures would in particular reduce the absolute probability of export, while the conditional ranking is less sensitive but still affected.[38]

No transmission dynamics: Risk estimates reflect the probability of a single importation and do not account for sustained local transmission in the receiving location.[153]

Limitations¶

Mobility-only baseline: The report uses the mobility framework only; no transmission-dynamics model is applied, and the values should not be read as forecasts of future case counts at any destination.[154] The model does not account for the probability of sustained local transmission in the receiving location.[153] Absolute likelihood of any international export, downstream local transmission, and outbreak burden at source are out of scope.[155]

Border-control measures not modelled: The analysis does not model country-level border-control measures, which would in particular affect absolute risk.[156] Conditional destination ranking is less sensitive but still affected, so the values should be interpreted as the mobility-only baseline.[157]

Traveller attributes and movement types: The model does not incorporate sociodemographic attributes of travellers, which may modulate both exposure risk at origin and care-seeking behaviour at destination.[158] Importation risk from repatriation flights, responder evacuations, or other ad-hoc operational movements is not part of the analysis.[159]

Independent importations and clusters: Related-case clusters are counted as one importation event, so the model may under-count distinct exposure events.[160]

Informal cross-border movement: Mobility data may not fully capture informal cross-border movement, which is substantial within the immediate cross-border region but is not the focus of the international-tail analysis.[161]

Small absolute risk not quantified: The unconditional probability of international export remains small and is further modulated by border-control interventions not captured in the model.[162]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: The report uses DRC data as of 7 October 2026[163], but the dataset type and sample size are not described. The report also cites a CFR of ≈ 48% in DRC as of 10 October 2026 (8,978 cases, 4,336 deaths).[164]

Auxiliary data: Global air travel patterns come from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) and the Official Airline Guide (OAG), giving passenger-level origin–destination flows between international airports.[165] These are complemented by short-scale commuting patterns capturing daily movements between adjacent subpopulations.[166] The incubation period used is 2–21 days, average ~11 days.[167] The report also notes that BDBV was first isolated in Uganda in 2007.[164]

Verheyden and Mudogo (12 Aug 2026)
Incidence-weighted force of infection for predicting first reported health-zone cases during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: a rolling-origin evaluation¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates which currently unaffected health zones in four DRC provinces are at highest near-term risk of reporting their first confirmed Bundibugyo virus case, in order to support prepositioning of response capacity. Four connectivity specifications — no connectivity term, road-distance, a gravity score, and an incidence-weighted force-of-infection (FOI) term — were fitted within an identical Bayesian hierarchical hazard architecture across 106 health zones in four affected provinces.[4] The FOI specification achieved the highest top-10 hit rate (42.6%), though on a global discrimination metric (AUC-PR), a model with no connectivity term performed as well as or better than any connectivity specification (0.437 vs. 0.409 for FOI).[168]

Estimate¶

This analysis does not estimate total outbreak size or case counts; its output is a ranked list of at-risk health zones by their estimated daily hazard of first reporting a confirmed case. The top-ranked zone, Rethy (Ituri), had a posterior median daily hazard of 0.095 (95% CrI [0.018, 0.295]), corresponding to roughly a 75% chance of reporting a first case within 14 days if current conditions persisted; the 20th-ranked zone’s daily hazard corresponds to roughly 4% over the same window.[169] On the pre-specified primary metric (top-10 hit rate), FOI was highest (42.6%), followed by OSRM-distance and gravity (both 32.8%), then baseline (29.5%).[170] On AUC-PR (a secondary metric), the baseline model with no connectivity term performed as well as or better than every connectivity specification (baseline 0.437 vs. FOI 0.409, gravity 0.399, OSRM-distance 0.239), and FOI’s advantage over baseline on this metric was not distinguishable from zero (−0.027, 95% CI [−0.274, 0.200]).[171] Across the kernel sensitivity grid of 8 alternative combinations, the resulting zone ranking correlated with the primary specification’s ranking at Spearman ρ = 0.90–0.99, with top-10 overlap of 9 or 10 out of 10 zones in every combination tested.[172]

Methods¶

Discrete-time hazard model with incidence-weighted force-of-infection (FOI): A discrete-time hazard model represents spatial connectivity through the observed incidence in every currently affected zone, propagated to at-risk zones through a road-network distance-decay kernel, referred to as an incidence-weighted spatial force-of-infection (FOI) hazard model.[173] Daily case data come from the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data repository; static covariates include WorldPop population estimates, OpenStreetMap/HOT health-facility points, Complex Crisis Vulnerability Index, and province-level ACLED conflict events; road-network travel times come from a national OSRM graph.[174] CDR/mobility data were not used, as DRC is not among the countries for which this is available.[175] The model is applied to the 106 health zones in Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo provinces. A sensitivity analysis varied the FOI kernel’s decay scale (φ ∈ {30, 60, 120} minutes) and smoothing window (1, 3, 7 days) across a grid of 8 alternative combinations, reporting ranking stability rather than re-selecting a best-performing specification.[176]

Architecture-matched comparison of four connectivity specifications: Four specifications of the connectivity covariate were compared within the identical model architecture: (1) a baseline with no connectivity term (static covariates only), (2) road-distance (log travel time to the nearest already-affected zone), (3) a population-weighted gravity score summed over all affected zones, and (4) the incidence-weighted FOI term as the primary specification.[177] Fitting all four within the identical architecture isolates what each connectivity term contributes beyond the static covariates and beyond each other.[178]

Rolling-origin pseudo-prospective evaluation: Eight weekly origins from 21 May to 9 July 2026 were used, each refit on data available through that origin and scored against zones reporting a first case within the following 14 days; top-10 hit rate — the proportion of true next-invading zones ranked in the model’s top 10 — was pre-specified as the primary metric.[179] Uncertainty quantification used a cluster bootstrap resampling whole origins with replacement (10,000 resamples).[180] Two further robustness checks were applied: leave-one-origin-out and a non-overlapping-origin subset of 4 origins spaced exactly 14 days apart.[181]

Exploratory growth-rate extension for already-affected zones: A secondary exploratory analysis examined near-term case growth for the 47 already-affected zones using a hierarchical negative-binomial growth-rate model, after an initial Poisson specification was found miscalibrated on rolling-origin backtesting.[182] This is not presented as a second validated model of comparable standing, and a combined invasion-plus-growth ranking is not presented as a validated decision tool, as that combined ranking has not itself been backtested.[183]

Assumptions¶

FOI kernel parameters: The FOI term uses a distance-decay kernel K(z,z’) = exp(−d(z,z’)/φ) with φ = 60 minutes as the default decay scale, and a 3-day trailing mean of new confirmed cases through day t−2 as the incidence weight.[184] The decay scale and smoothing window were not tuned against performance; across a grid of 8 alternative combinations (φ ∈ {30, 60, 120} minutes × window ∈ {1, 3, 7} days), the resulting zone ranking correlated with the primary specification at Spearman ρ = 0.90–0.99, with top-10 overlap of 9 or 10 out of 10 zones in every combination, indicating the ranking is stable across plausible kernel choices.[185]

Temporal lag to avoid leakage: Same-day leakage is addressed by using only incidence through day t−2, never day t or t−1, to construct the FOI covariate.[186] An earlier, same-day (non-lagged) specification yielded a FOI coefficient of +0.610 [0.43, 0.79] compared to +0.357 [0.16, 0.55] after applying the lag, indicating same-day leakage had inflated the apparent effect by roughly 40%.[187]

Outcome definition: The outcome modelled is a zone’s first reported confirmed case, not the date of biological introduction of the virus; first confirmation reflects viral introduction, local transmission, detection, testing access, reporting capacity, and retrospective case reclassification jointly, and the model cannot separate these.[188]

Static covariates and structural form: Health-facility density (β = +0.486, [0.245, 0.734]) and population (β = +0.400, [0.087, 0.720]) are associated with hazard at the 95% credible level and are included as structural inputs; socioeconomic deprivation (+0.326, [−0.074, 0.754]) and province-level conflict exposure (+0.156, [−0.640, 0.900]) were not distinguishable from zero.[189] Conflict exposure is measured only at province level across four provinces, alongside a province random effect estimated from the same four groups; this covariate’s estimate is described as exploratory.[190]

Data-vintage leakage and pseudo-prospective evaluation: Data-vintage leakage — whether case counts available for a historical date already reflect corrections made after that date — cannot be ruled out, since only the final, most recently corrected dataset is held rather than dated historical snapshots; the rolling-origin evaluation is therefore described as pseudo-prospective throughout, not a true contemporaneous test.[191]

Province random effect: A non-centred province random effect is included in the linear predictor alongside a piecewise-constant weekly baseline evolving as a random walk and weakly informative priors.[192]

Limitations¶

Pseudo-prospective evaluation and data-vintage leakage: Because historical snapshots of the surveillance dataset at each rolling-origin date were not available, the authors cannot rule out that retrospective data revision is reflected in what the evaluation treats as contemporaneously known information; the rolling-origin evaluation is therefore described as pseudo-prospective throughout, reserving the term prospective for the genuinely pre-registered future verification.[193]

Outcome reflects detection as well as introduction: The outcome modelled is first reported confirmed case, not the unobserved date of viral introduction; these differ to the extent that introduction, local transmission, detection, testing access, and reporting capacity differ across zones, and the model cannot separate these mechanisms. This matters specifically for the health-facility-density covariate, whose positive association with hazard may partly or wholly reflect greater detection capacity in better-served zones rather than, or in addition to, genuinely greater introduction risk.[194]

Absence of mobile-phone mobility data: Existing approaches to spatial spread typically rely on mobile-phone call detail record data, which a systematic review found available in only a small number of African countries, not including DRC; CDR data were therefore not used in this analysis.[195][175]

Statistical uncertainty in the primary comparison: The top-10 hit rate comparison against road-distance reaches only the boundary of conventional significance (CI lower bound 0.000); the authors state they would not describe this as a robust result on its own and rely on convergent evidence across the primary metric, the sensitivity grid, and the leave-one-origin-out and non-overlapping-origin checks collectively.[196]

AUC-PR divergence: On AUC-PR, the baseline model with no connectivity term performed as well as or better than every connectivity specification; the authors report this plainly, noting that a global discrimination metric rewards correctly ranking the bulk of zones that will not invade soon, which static covariates alone appear to do reasonably well, while the connectivity terms’ distinguishable contribution is specifically to sharpening the top of the ranking.[197]

Conflict exposure measured only at province level: Conflict exposure is measured only at province level across four provinces, alongside a province random effect estimated from the same four groups; the authors state this covariate’s estimate should be read as exploratory.[190]

Growth-rate extension not combined with hazard model: The growth-rate extension has not been backtested as a combined ranking with the hazard model, and the authors do not present one for that reason.[198]

Fixed modelling choices not evaluated: Fixed choices not evaluated in this analysis include the OSRM travel-time transformation and the province-level (rather than zone-level) conflict aggregation.[199]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Daily case data come from the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data repository (Mbulayi et al., 2026).[200] The study period covers 14 May to 26 July 2026, yielding 5,727 zone-day observations and 47 first-case events across the risk set.[201][202]

Auxiliary data: Static covariates include WorldPop population estimates, OpenStreetMap/HOT health-facility points, Complex Crisis Vulnerability Index, and province-level ACLED conflict events.[203] Road-network travel times were derived from a national OSRM graph.[204] CDR/mobility data were not used, as DRC is not among the countries for which such data are available.[175] An independent Flowminder-based mobility analysis (Bangelesa et al., 2026, as summarised in Walekhwa et al., 2026) found the outbreak’s three epicentre zones among the top 5% of DRC health zones nationally on mobility intensity; this was used as external, indirect support for the general connectivity premise, not as a model input.[205]

Li et al. (11 Aug 2026)
Dynamics, Optimal Control, and Spillover Risk of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis develops a compartmental transmission model (SEIDR: susceptible-exposed-infectious-deceased-recovered) to characterize the early transmission dynamics of the 2026 BDBV outbreak in the DRC and to estimate the risk that the outbreak spreads internationally through population mobility. The model incorporates three categories of interventions—public self-protection, safe burial, and treatment and convalescence—to assess early transmission dynamics, the current epidemic trajectory, and cross-border spillover risk, and to inform the formulation of control strategies.[206] Spillover risk is separately estimated using International Migrant Stock data and Facebook IP-based mobility data with the Prophet forecasting model[207], and the analysis reports that four countries were identified as very high risk at the end of July[208], a number the authors project would grow substantially under a “status quo” scenario but stay comparatively contained under an optimized control strategy.

Estimate¶

The paper’s headline model output is not an outbreak-size estimate in isolation but a set of counterfactual/projected cumulative infection trajectories tied to control scenarios. Under the fitted (actual) trajectory, cumulative confirmed cases increased from 33 to 3,674[209] during the observation period (18 May–31 July). Had the derived optimal control strategy been applied from the estimated transmission start date, the simulated cumulative number of infections as of 31 July would have been approximately 135 cases, representing a 96.33% reduction compared with the 3,674 cases actually reported during the same period[210]. Projecting forward from the actual 31 July epidemic size under the optimal control strategy, cumulative infections would reach 4,372 (95% CI: 4,300–4,450) by 31 August and 4,397 (95% CI: 4,325–4,474) by 30 September, after which the epidemic would enter a plateau phase, with only one additional case by 31 October[211]. By contrast, under the status quo control scenario, the epidemic was projected to continue rising until the end of April 2027[212]. The basic reproduction number, a related transmission-intensity estimate, was ℛ0 = 1.83 (95% CI: 1.81–1.84), of which ℛ0I = 1.14 (62.18%) and ℛ0D = 0.69 (37.82%)[213].

Methods¶

SEIDR compartmental transmission model: Building upon the classical SEIR framework, and incorporating the specific transmission characteristics of Ebola virus and the public health realities in the affected region, the model was extended to include a deceased compartment (D), resulting in a SEIDR structure[214]. It was fitted to DRC national cumulative confirmed case counts to estimate the reproduction number and its living-case versus corpse-mediated components, and to infer the start date of sustained transmission.

NSGA-II combined with Pontryagin’s Minimum Principle (optimal control): To overcome shortcomings of conventional PMP-based indirect methods, the authors propose a hybrid solution strategy combining PMP with non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II), using a global optimisation algorithm to generate high-quality initial guesses that guide PMP iterations towards rapid convergence to the globally optimal solution.[215] This produces a time-varying optimal control strategy, with adjustments every two weeks[216], applied to the DRC-level SEIDR model.

Migration-based spillover/importation risk model: To assess the risk of Ebola virus disease spreading beyond the outbreak country (DRC) to other regions, international migration data were incorporated to evaluate cross-border spread risk, assuming homogeneous mixing and equal probability of out-migration, with the number of imported cases modelled as following a binomial distribution based on cumulative out-migrants, cumulative confirmed cases in the DRC, and total DRC population.[217] Annual International Migrant Stock data served as the baseline measure of population connectivity, with monthly outflow proportions estimated using Facebook IP-address-based migration data for 2019–2022 and a Prophet forecasting model to capture seasonal patterns and trend changes.[218] This method produces country-level importation risk estimates and rankings for destinations worldwide, run separately under status-quo and optimized-control scenarios for August–December 2026.

Assumptions¶

Start date of sustained transmission: the model treats the transmission onset as unknown and searched over a range; the possible start date of sustained transmission was set to range between 24 March and 24 April, generating 32 candidate start-date scenarios[219], with 28 March identified as the optimal fitting start date (R²=0.7586), and start dates between 31 March and 3 April also yielding good fitting performance (R²>0.7)[220].

Homogeneous mixing and national-population susceptible pool: the model assumes homogeneous mixing of the population in the affected country and equal probability of out-migration for all individuals[221], and uses the total national population of the DRC as the susceptible population base, without accounting for geographic clustering of the outbreak or the effect of population mobility on contact patterns[222].

Worst-case importation assumption: the use of cumulative cases rather than active infections represents a worst-case scenario assumption, in which all reported infected individuals are considered potentially infectious[41], driving the binomial importation-probability calculation.

Intervention parameters (θ, ρ, μ): the model’s control levers are calibrated with fitted values of public self-protection (θ) fitted at 0.2332, safe burial rate (ρ) fitted at 0.2664, and treatment/recovery rate (μ) fitted at 0.3227[223], with thresholds identified where ℛ0 fell below 1 when θ exceeded 58.12%, and ℛ0I < 1 when θ exceeded 32.65%[224], ℛ0 < 1 only when μ > 98.46% but ℛ0I < 1 when μ > 43.31%[225], and ℛ0D < 1 when ρ exceeded 20.09%[226]. Sensitivity ranges for these parameters were constrained: the ranges for θ and μ were set to [0, 1], and the range for ρ was set to [0.1, 1][227], because ℛ0D is undefined when ρ = 0.

Risk-tier thresholds: country-level spillover classification is based on the normal distribution of importation risk probabilities as of end-July, stratified into four levels: 0 < Pb,t < 16.38% as low risk, 16.38% ≤ Pb,t < 43.68% as moderate risk, 43.68% ≤ Pb,t < 70.98% as high risk, and 70.98% ≤ Pb,t < 1 as very high risk[228].

Limitations¶

National-level population base obscures spatial and mobility effects on transmission: the model used the total national population of the DRC as the susceptible population base, without accounting for geographic clustering of the outbreak or the effect of population mobility on contact patterns, which may lead to systematic underestimation of the transmission rate parameter β.[222]

Optimal control strategy is theoretical and unvalidated operationally: although the optimised control functions provide mathematically derived theoretical optima, their operational effectiveness and practical implementation in the actual outbreak context require further validation.[229]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: daily cumulative confirmed case counts for the DRC were extracted from WHO’s Daily epidemiological update on acute public health events: Ebola disease—Bundibugyo virus, compiled by COUSP-DRC, retrieved as a complete time series from the start of the outbreak up to the study cut-off date (31 July 2026)[230]. Background totals cite 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths reported as of 11 August[231], and reported imported cases: Uganda has reported two imported cases with 20 cumulative confirmed cases domestically; France has reported one imported case with no local secondary transmission[232].

Auxiliary data: Population data were obtained from the World Population Prospects 2024, published by the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division, covering the total populations of the DRC and potential risk-importation countries[233]. Cross-border mobility data were derived from the International Migrant Stock 2024: Destination and Origin, published by the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, with monthly allocation weights determined according to reference, to estimate the volume and spatial distribution of outflows from the DRC to neighbouring countries and major destination countries.[234] Monthly out-migration data from the DRC based on Facebook IP addresses for the period 2019–2022[235] were used with the Prophet model. Historical outbreak parameters were also drawn from the literature: the 2007 outbreak in Uganda reported 116 confirmed cases with 39 deaths, with a basic reproduction number estimated at 1.53; the 2012 outbreak in the DRC reported 77 cases.[236]

Klein et al. (2 Aug 2026)
Model-guided placement of decentralized diagnostics for spatial control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola epidemic¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

The analysis estimates how many future deaths and new health-zone invasions in DRC could be averted by placing decentralized PCR laboratories and postmortem rapid tests ahead of the outbreak frontier, rather than where cases are already concentrated. It fits a Bayesian spatial branching process to public situation reports through 2 August 2026, using Flowminder movement data and a latent-burden anchor.[237] It then replays 2,000 posterior trees with 5-100 zone-level PCR laboratories, deployment delays of 0-180 days, and postmortem RDT coverage.[238] Speed dominated: 35 PCR laboratories averted a median 49% of future deaths if deployed immediately, 38% after 14 days, and 11% after 60 days[239]. With a 30-day delay, model-informed placement averted 18-33% of future deaths with 20-100 laboratories, versus 1-8% under random placement.[240] All results are conditional on an assumed national response ramp, not a fitted one.

Estimate¶

The analysis does not estimate current outbreak size as its headline. Its headline results are deaths averted under diagnostic scenarios. It does report a simulated status-quo projection, conditional on the assumed national response ramp. Under the status quo plus the selected national response ramp, the simulated outbreak reached a median of 31,615 cumulative infections, 14,256 deaths, and 110 invaded health zones by 540 days after 2 August 2026.[241] No intervals are given for these medians. Of those deaths, a median 4,816 were already locked in by the calibration horizon, leaving a median 9,360 future deaths that could still be averted.[242] The calibration matched 3,802 cumulative confirmed cases and 1,707 cumulative confirmed deaths at 2 August 2026.[243]

Intervention results, as a share of deaths still avertable after the cutoff, are as follows.

  • With 35 PCR laboratories, a median 49% of future deaths were averted if deployed immediately, 38% after 14 days and 11% after 60 days, with 90% prediction intervals of 30-65%, 23-53% and 5-20%.[239]

  • With a 30-day delay, model-informed placement averted 18-33% of deaths with 20-100 laboratories, versus 1-8% under random placement.[240]

  • Postmortem RDTs raised future deaths averted from 26% to 41% with 20 laboratories, a 14-day delay and 75% coverage.[244]

For spatial spread, the status quo seeded a median 32 new health zones after 2 August 2026, versus 29, 26 and 25 with 20, 50 and 100 model-placed laboratories.[245]

Methods¶

Bayesian spatial branching process (status-quo calibration): This is an individual-level stochastic model in which each infection has a parent, a health zone, and detection, isolation and burial states. The epidemic was simulated as an individual-level stochastic branching process.[246] Each offspring infection stays in the local zone or jumps to another zone drawn from Flowminder outflows.[247] It was fitted to the INSP/INRB-UMIE situation-report time series for DRC nationally (health-zone level). It also used a latent-burden anchor from the EpiForecasts BVD-OutbreakSize analysis.[248] Calibration used a pseudo-marginal MCMC sampler.[249] It yields joint posterior samples of parameters and epidemic trajectories. A possible national reduction in transmission after the calibration horizon was added to represent broad behavioral change and non-diagnostic response.[250] This produced one plausible future at roughly West-Africa scale and was not a posterior estimate of future response strength.[251]

Matched counterfactual replay of diagnostic scenarios: The same posterior trees were replayed with and without new PCR laboratories and postmortem RDTs. Each intervention scenario prunes only the transmissions that earlier detection, isolation, tracing or safe burial would have prevented. Both simulations shared the same per-case random numbers.[252] Budgets of 5 to 100 laboratories were placed in health zones not served by existing laboratories.[253] A lazy CELF optimizer selected laboratories by marginal deaths averted, with random placement as the comparator.[254] Deployment delays of 0, 14, 30, 60, 90, 120 and 180 days were tested.[255] RDT scenarios raised postmortem testing to 50% or 75% coverage, either inside the PCR footprint or everywhere.[256] A sample-transport sensitivity analysis let unserved zones ship specimens to the nearest new laboratory.[257]

Assumptions¶

National response ramp: This is the assumption the results depend on most. A national reduction in transmission after 2 August 2026 stands in for broad behavioral change and non-diagnostic response.[250] It was chosen against a 540-day West Africa anchor. The primary scenario reached half its effect after 90 days, with a final scale of 0.25 and Hill exponent 2.[258][259] It is chosen rather than fitted because the likelihood is blind to its parameters inside the fitted window.[260] The authors state that much faster non-diagnostic control would leave fewer deaths to avert, while larger or more sustained transmission would widen the PCR placement window.[261] They expect the relative ranking of strategies to be less sensitive than the absolute benefit.[262]

Natural history and transmission: The generation interval is gamma with mean 15.3 days and SD 9.3 days.[263] The incubation period is lognormal with mean 6.3 days and SD 3.5 days.[264] Onset-to-death has a gamma distribution with mean 12 days, and onset-to-recovery a gamma with mean 16 days.[265] Also fixed is the assumption that 37% of a fatal case’s transmission potential falls in a 0.8-day postmortem period. These were varied only in scenario sensitivity checks.[266] Offspring dispersion k is fixed at 0.372 after weak identification in earlier fits.[267] The posterior median R0 was 2.63, the median fitted infection fatality ratio 0.46, and the latest Rt 1.11.[268]

Spatial movement: Between-zone jumps use a single fitted jump probability shared across zones, with Flowminder flows setting relative destination probabilities.[269] The median jump probability was 0.19.[270] The model places cases where infection occurred and has no explicit referral to regional hospitals, nosocomial amplification, or facility-level transmission.[271] Susceptible depletion is ignored, which the authors call reasonable at the fitted attack rates but a limitation for very prolonged or very large trajectories.[272]

Laboratory catchment and diagnosis: The primary analysis assumed routine sample transport between health zones is highly challenging, so a laboratory primarily serves its own zone.[273] Zones with existing laboratories were excluded from new placement, leaving 462 candidates.[274] A sensitivity analysis lets unserved zones ship specimens to the nearest new laboratory.[257] PCR sensitivity is not modelled as a separate failure process; a sampled true infection is assumed PCR-confirmed.[275] Tracing is an offspring-level probability rather than an explicit contact graph.[276] Tracing from a PCR-confirmed index was inferred to intercept a median 69% of its offspring.[277]

Postmortem RDT and care-seeking: RDT scenarios raise postmortem testing to at least 50% or 75% coverage of otherwise undiagnosed deaths and assume 80% sensitivity.[278] A positive RDT is assumed to lead to safe burial without additional modeled delay.[279] The scenarios assume demand for decentralized care. The authors say limited care seeking would weaken the mechanism.[280][281]

Limitations¶

Stylized model structure: The authors describe the model as intentionally stylized. It ignores susceptible depletion, omits onward transmission after importations to neighboring countries, represents contact tracing as a probability on true offspring, and has no healthcare-facility compartment or nosocomial channel.[282] These choices soften facility-level siting conclusions. The model should be read as ranking broad frontier risk and mechanism sizes, not as a deterministic list of which clinics must receive devices.[283]

Assumed rather than fitted response ramp: The national response ramp is chosen, not fitted, so all diagnostic effects are marginal to it.[284] The size of the baseline future affects the numerical scale of every counterfactual.[285] The authors state that the exact timing of the benefit decline is tied to the assumed future response trajectory.[286]

Catchment and transport assumptions: The intervention analysis was limited to one primary sample-transport assumption.[287] If a zone assigned to an existing laboratory is not served quickly in practice, the model would wrongly give it a high PCR probability and conclude a new laboratory there has little value.[288]

Fixed-allocation and national objective: The placement result is a fixed allocation problem, with the optimizer given the posterior at one decision time.[289] Field placement is more reactive.[290] The objective minimized burden inside DRC only.[291]

RDT pathways and cost not represented: Faster notification from postmortem positives back to local awareness is not represented, so RDT effects are one-sided lower bounds for any pathway that would also accelerate recognition or tracing.[292] The model considers epidemiologic benefit but not cost, so it cannot determine whether a given mix of laboratories, staff, transport and burial teams is cost-effective.[293]

Care-seeking demand: Limited care seeking would weaken the mechanism by which closer diagnostics find cases earlier.[281]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: The public INSP/INRB-UMIE record contained 3,802 confirmed cases and 1,707 confirmed deaths across 51 health zones by 2 August 2026.[294] The data were pinned locally at SitRep 81, with data to 3 August 2026.[295] Laboratory activation dates, approximate PCR turnaround tiers, early Bunia and Rwampara capacity, and Ituri PCR throughput anchors were compiled from the laboratory sections of public situation reports.[296]

Auxiliary data:

  • Spatial spread used the HDX Flowminder DRC origin-destination matrix from March 2026.[5]

  • Province-level ACLED event rates for the 12 months ending 25 July 2026 were used to derive an operating-disruption score.[297]

  • The latent-burden anchor from the EpiForecasts BVD-OutbreakSize analysis uses INSP situation reports and Uganda export data.[248]

  • The generation interval (mean 15.3 days, SD 9.3 days) is the West African Ebola Zaire serial-interval estimate from the WHO Ebola Response Team (2014).[263]

  • The incubation period uses the BDBV mean from the 2007-2008 Uganda outbreak.[264]

  • The forward response ramp was chosen against a 540-day anchor based on the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola Zaire confirmed-case burden.[258]

Verheyden and Mudogo (20 Jul 2026)
Returning to school during Ebola: an exploratory health-zone framework for scenario-based school-system introduction pressure during the September 2026 rentrée in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates where in eastern DRC an infected school-age child is most likely to reach a school before being recognised and isolated during the September 2026 school return, expressed as expected introduction pressure for each health zone over a one-week window[298]. It combines recent reported transmission, estimated school-age exposure and attendance, a surveillance/interception probability, and mobility-based importation[299]. The base scenario gives a combined expected pressure of 10.97 across six provinces, with a sensitivity range of 5.56–20.97[300], and Bunia, Rwampara and Nizi rank highest[301]. It is a prioritisation tool for school-linked surveillance and readiness, not a forecast and not an outbreak-size or international-importation estimate.

Estimate¶

The analysis does not estimate outbreak size. Its headline quantity is scenario-based expected introduction pressure for infected school-age children reaching schools. At the 11 August cut-off, the base specification gave a combined expected count of 10.97 school-system introductions across the six-province scope during the modelled week.[302] The median across 10,000 sensitivity draws was 11.17, with a 2.5th–97.5th percentile sensitivity range of 5.56–20.97.[303] This is an expectation under model assumptions, not a forecast that exactly eleven infected pupils will attend school.[304]

The pressure was geographically concentrated. Ituri accounted for about 8.47 of the 10.97, North Kivu about 1.39 and Haut-Uélé about 1.03.[305] Bunia had the highest base value (λ=2.08; P≥1=87.4%), followed by Rwampara (λ=1.84; 84.1%) and Nizi (λ=1.32; 73.4%)[306]. Katwa and Nia Nia each had a modelled probability of at least one introduction of approximately 50%.[307] The median imported component was 1.31, with a sensitivity range of 0.51–3.28.[308] The main driver of the spread was the pre-recognition school-entry probability: changing baseline q from 0.10 to 0.50 moved the total from approximately 4.39 to 21.95[309].

The ranking was more stable than the counts. Bunia, Rwampara, Nizi, Katwa and Nia Nia stayed in the top ten in essentially all simulations.[310] The retrospective validation results are as follows.

  • Seven-day local pressure gave a pooled ROC-AUC of 0.848, rising to 0.885 with the 14-day measure.[311][312]

  • Adding mobility raised it to 0.952 with seven-day source pressure and 0.953 with fourteen-day pressure.[313]

  • Of 24 newly affected zones, 13 (54.2%) were in the top 10 and 18 (75.0%) in the top 20 mobility-ranked unaffected zones.[314]

Methods¶

Scenario-based health-zone introduction pressure model: This is an exploratory calculation applied to DRC health zones across the six provinces. It takes the most recent seven-day reported case count and projects it forward as one week of cases[315]. Projected cases are multiplied by the assumed 5–17-year case share and expected attendance, then by the probability that an infected child reaches school before recognition, isolation or exclusion[316]. The result is expressed as an expected count and converted to a model-implied scenario probability with 1 − exp(−λ)[317]. A 14-day weekly-equivalent pressure measure was examined as a robustness check.[315]

Directed mobility-based imported pressure: This component applies to destination health zones within the same 151-zone study area. Pressure at each origin is distributed to destinations using Flowminder and IOM origin–destination shares and scenario movement fractions[318], and the destination’s interception adjustment is then applied[319]. This separates local from imported pressure and produces a mobility-derived warning signal for zones with no recent local cases.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis: This ran 10,000 Monte Carlo draws, with the 5–17 case share, attendance, baseline interception probability and mobility fractions drawn from split-triangular distributions[320]. Week-to-week case-count variability was represented by a Poisson draw.[321] It varies inputs to the same model rather than changing the method.

Retrospective validation of geographic components: This tests the local-pressure and mobility layers against subsequent reported activity. Only information available at each cut-off was used, with activity assessed over the following seven days.[322] The two outcomes were any reported increase in cumulative confirmed cases, and the first confirmed case in a previously unaffected health zone[323]. Performance was summarised with ROC-AUC, average precision, top-10 and top-20 capture, and Spearman correlation.[324] A secondary exploratory comparison tested three nested specifications[325]: local pressure alone, local pressure plus surveillance and access modifiers, and the same with mobility.

Separate CFR analysis and contextual SitRep synthesis: CFR was analysed separately using empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward a provincial comparator, treated only as a descriptive signal that did not alter the ranking[326]. The ten most recent national situation reports were reviewed qualitatively, with no contextual theme converted into a model weight.[327]

Assumptions¶

Pre-recognition school-entry probability (q): The base value is 0.25, with low and high scenarios of 0.10 and 0.50.[328] Health-zone values are adjusted by analyst-specified modifiers for contact follow-up, testing access, health-site density, school-response activity and data quality, clipped between 0.05 and 0.75.[329] These weights are not fitted coefficients.[330] The authors identify this as the dominant uncertainty: moving baseline q from 0.10 to 0.50 changed the total from about 4.39 to 21.95[309].

School-age exposure inputs: The population aged 5–17 is set at a national share of 31.96%.[331] Attendance is 56.6% at base, with low and high values of 45% and 70%.[332] The 5–17 case share is 13.17% and was varied from 10% to 16%.[333] These are exposure assumptions rather than observed attendance on 1 September.[334]

One-week continuation and Poisson transformation: The next school-week case burden is projected from the most recent seven-day case count.[315] Converting λ to a probability uses a Poisson assumption that is not tested for clustered household, mobility or school-linked events.[335] The authors state it is not an empirically calibrated probability forecast.[317]

Mobility treatment: Origin–destination entries are normalised across destinations in the study matrix, and origins with no usable row contribute no imported pressure.[336] Flowminder and IOM flows are treated as additive, which may double-count some movement; a Flowminder-only sensitivity reduced total λ only from 10.974 to 10.736.[337] Plausible changes in mobility scaling moved the total much less than q.[338]

CFR and context kept outside λ: Crude CFRs were not used as transmission drivers.[339] No contextual theme was converted into a numerical model weight.[340]

Sensitivity distributions: Structural assumptions were drawn from split-triangular distributions with the base value as the median.[341] The Poisson step is a simple process-variation device that does not establish that introductions are independently Poisson.[342]

Limitations¶

Calibration and interpretation of probabilities: The probabilities are model-implied scenario probabilities rather than calibrated forecasts.[343] The sensitivity ranges are not calibrated confidence or predictive intervals.[344] The result is a pre-rentrée snapshot rather than a direct observation of September attendance.[345]

Extrapolated denominators and borrowed inputs: School and pupil denominators are extrapolated rather than drawn from a harmonised health-zone school census, and the 5–17 case share comes from a national snapshot rather than health-zone-specific age incidence.[346] Contact-follow-up and alert-investigation indicators are affected by reporting completeness.[347]

Mobility data coverage and interpretation: Mobility data describe population movement rather than observed pupil or teacher travel, and missing or redacted flows can generate false reassurance.[348] Vuhovi received a zero mobility score because it was absent from the Flowminder matrix, a coverage failure showing that low modelled imported risk is not proof of no importation risk.[349] Mobility may partly capture population size, urbanisation or reporting intensity, and no population, distance or urbanisation comparator model was added.[350] Data coverage was also uneven, with 96 of 151 health zones flagged as having no health-zone case series.[351]

Scope of the validation: The retrospective validation assesses reported health-zone activity, not an infected child actually entering a school.[352] It cannot fully distinguish biological spread from differences in testing access, reporting completeness, insecurity, response attention or data connectivity.[353] The bootstrap intervals reflect variation across a small number of origins and are not external-validation confidence intervals.[354] The nested-specification comparison does not create an independent temporal or spatial holdout.[355]

Reproducibility boundaries: The package does not fully reconstruct the original rolling-origin score matrices from dated health-zone histories.[356] It also does not constitute an independently double-extracted SitRep audit trail.[357]

No within-school transmission or school-level modelling: The study does not model within-school secondary transmission.[358] The authors state available evidence is sufficient to identify these mechanisms but not to calibrate a defensible school-level transmission model across 151 health zones.[359] Urban/rural school conditions are not modelled as a separate coefficient because comparable school-level data are not available.[360]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Epidemiological data came from DRC national SitReps and the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data repository, which manually transcribes SitRep indicators.[361] The model used recent seven-day reported case incidence as the principal epidemic-pressure signal[362]. The age share came from the latest usable standardised SitRep demographic snapshot (455 of 3,454 cases; 13.17%)[333]. Health-zone case histories for validation were reconstructed from a reconciled direct-PDF series[363]. The primary validation included 1,208 health-zone–origin observations, of which 200 showed activity in the following seven days[364]. It also included 930 unaffected candidate observations and 24 first-health-zone events.[365] The contextual review used the ten most recent national SitReps (31 July–11 August 2026).[366] Of 151 analytical health zones, 96 were flagged as having no health-zone case series and 55 as OK/review.[351]

Auxiliary data: Health-zone population denominators came from the WorldPop layer in the repository.[367] The school-age share (31.96%) and attendance values (base 56.6%) were derived from UNICEF/UN population age bands and UNICEF education indicators.[368] Directed mobility came from Flowminder origin–destination data and IOM displacement flows in the repository.[6] The Flowminder matrix had nonzero outgoing rows for 132 health zones and the IOM matrix for 43.[369] Documentary context included May 2026 Ministry of Education instructions to schools[370] and older benchmarks such as MICS 2018 indicators cited by UNICEF and Education Cannot Wait[371]. These contextual items were used for interpretation, not as model inputs.

Bouhentala & Kadir (15 Jul 2026)
Epidemiological Analysis of the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak and Rapid Risk Assessment for North Africa and Europe¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis assesses the risk of introduction and onward transmission of the 2026 BDBV outbreak into North Africa and Europe, using publicly available aggregate surveillance data synthesized through mid-July 2026. Risk was assessed across four dimensions: introduction likelihood, conditional onward-transmission likelihood, impact, and confidence.[372] Introduction likelihood was assessed as very low to low for North Africa and very low for the general European population, with delayed recognition in routine healthcare identified as the principal scenario for limited secondary transmission.[16]

Estimate¶

This analysis does not produce a quantitative outbreak-size estimate for DRC. It reports observed surveillance counts as descriptive figures rather than model-derived estimates. As of 15 July 2026, the DRC had reported 2,124 laboratory-confirmed cases, 828 deaths among confirmed cases, 390 reported recoveries, and 725 patients hospitalised in isolation, across 46 of 140 health zones in five provinces.[373] The headline epidemiological trend finding is a notification-rate ratio: the aggregate rate was 35.9 per day during 2–29 June (970 notifications over 27 days; exact counting interval 33.7–38.3) and 47.4 per day during 1–15 July (664 over 14 days; 43.9–51.2), yielding a July-to-June notification-rate ratio of 1.32 (counting-model 95% interval 1.20–1.46).[374] For importation risk, the analysis cites an external ECDC estimate rather than producing its own: ECDC estimated approximately one importation per 23,000–24,000 travellers from the principal outbreak region (90% uncertainty interval one per 13,000–54,000), and under a hypothetical scenario of 100 travellers during 11–25 June, estimated a 0.45% probability of at least one importation (90% uncertainty interval 0.20%–0.85%).[375]

Methods¶

Rapid public-health risk assessment using aggregate surveillance data: This was a rapid public-health analysis of publicly available aggregate surveillance data and official risk assessments, drawing on WHO Disease Outbreak News, WHO/IHR statements and technical guidance, ECDC surveillance and modelling reports, WHO regional offices, national ministry-of-health dashboards, and peer-reviewed primary studies for historical BDBV outbreaks, viral persistence, and candidate countermeasures.[376] Airline sources were used only to establish the existence of plausible routes and not to estimate passenger volumes.[377] This approach covers DRC nationally (with provincial detail for Ituri) as the source population, and North Africa and Europe as destination geographies.

Interval-specific notification-rate analysis: Cumulative confirmed DRC counts were indexed by reporting date rather than symptom-onset date, and interval-specific average notification rates were calculated as the change in cumulative confirmed cases divided by the number of days between reports, with exact 95% Poisson counting intervals calculated using the Garwood method.[378] The notification-rate ratio comparing 1–15 July with 2–29 June was calculated on the log scale using SE[log(RR)] = √(1/C₁ + 1/C₀).[379] No reproduction number was estimated because onset-date line-list data were unavailable.[380]

Structured qualitative risk rating: Risk was separated into four dimensions — introduction likelihood, conditional onward-transmission likelihood after an importation, impact if detection was delayed, and confidence in the judgement — with categories treated as comparative reference classes rather than calibrated probabilities; boundary ratings such as ‘very low to low’ were retained when the evidence did not support a more precise classification.[381] The ratings were calibrated against WHO’s 6 June assessment, which classified risk as very high in the DRC, high in Uganda and bordering countries, low in the remainder of the WHO African Region, and low globally.[382]

Assumptions¶

Reporting-date indexing and its limitations: The Poisson counting intervals describe counting variation only and do not incorporate systematic uncertainty from backlogs, under-ascertainment, changing testing, or reporting delays.[383] The observed increase in notification rates cannot be interpreted as a direct measure of biological acceleration, as WHO noted that expanded surveillance, testing, and diagnostic capacity contributed to rising reported counts, and newly reported cases could include backlogs.[29]

Risk ratings as comparative reference classes rather than calibrated probabilities: Risk categories are comparative reference classes rather than calibrated probabilities.[384] Passenger-volume and confidential readiness data were unavailable[385], so country ratings rest on route availability, occupational exposure patterns, and qualitative preparedness indicators rather than quantified traveller volumes.

Transmission requires direct contact: A recognised symptomatic case can usually be contained because transmission requires direct contact with blood or other body fluids, contaminated materials, or the body of a deceased case rather than ordinary casual proximity.[386] This structural assumption underpins the low conditional sustained-transmission rating for North Africa and Europe.

Border screening ineffectiveness during incubation: An incubating traveller can cross a border while asymptomatic because people are not considered infectious before symptom onset and the incubation period can extend to 21 days; temperature screening may detect some symptomatic travellers but cannot exclude infection during incubation.[387]

Itinerary concealment risk: A final departure airport may conceal earlier travel to eastern DRC; triage therefore requires a complete 21-day itinerary and exposure history.[388]

Cumulative doubling time not treated as a transmission signal: Arithmetic cumulative doubling times were treated as descriptive properties of the cumulative curve and not as evidence of changes in transmission.[389]

Limitations¶

Dependence on public aggregate data: The main limitation is dependence on public aggregate data; reporting dates do not represent symptom onset, and the analysis could not estimate time-varying reproduction numbers, serial intervals, onset-to-isolation delays, household secondary-attack rates, health-zone-specific growth, or intervention effects.[31]

Incomplete auxiliary inputs for importation assessment: Passenger volumes, traveller occupations, deployment rosters, medevac activity, and country-specific laboratory and referral readiness were incomplete; country ratings were therefore comparative judgements rather than calibrated probabilities.[48]

Counting intervals understating true uncertainty: Notification rates remain composite measures of infection, care seeking, alert investigation, specimen transport, laboratory capacity, retrospective death investigation, and reporting; the exact Poisson intervals are therefore deliberately described as counting-model intervals rather than complete epidemiological uncertainty intervals.[390]

CFR interpretation caution: The rise in confirmed-case CFR is compatible with maturation of outcomes among previously active cases, retrospective confirmation of deaths, delayed presentation, preferential detection of severe disease, delayed recovery reporting, and changes in testing or death investigation; it should not be interpreted as a time-resolved measure of clinical virulence.[391]

Unresolved status discrepancy in DRC counts: The published status totals did not fully reconcile — 828 deaths, 390 recoveries, and 725 hospitalised patients summed to 1,943, leaving 181 of 2,124 confirmed cases outside those categories — and public reports did not define the status of these cases; potential explanations include pending admission or outcome reconciliation, transfers, and reporting lags, but no category could be assigned without line-list data.[392]

Time-stamped analysis: The analysis was time-stamped and may be superseded by subsequent official reports.[393]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Public surveillance reports from WHO, ECDC, Africa CDC, national ministries of health, and peer-reviewed sources were synthesised through 15–17 July 2026.[394] The main DRC trajectory used laboratory-confirmed cases and deaths among confirmed cases; suspected, probable, and confirmed categories were not summed across reports because individuals and deaths can be reclassified as investigations progress.[395] Uganda’s official dashboard as of 17 July reported 20 confirmed cases, two confirmed deaths, 18 recoveries, and no current admissions.[396] WHO’s jurisdictional accounting on 17 July comprised 2,145 confirmed cases globally: 2,124 in the DRC, 20 in Uganda, and one in France, with 830 confirmed-case deaths.[397]

Auxiliary data: Peer-reviewed primary studies were used for historical BDBV outbreaks, viral persistence, and candidate countermeasures.[398] Airline sources were used only to establish the existence of plausible routes and not to estimate passenger volumes.[377] ECDC Monte Carlo importation summaries (approximately one importation per 23,000–24,000 travellers, with 90% uncertainty interval one per 13,000–54,000) were referenced as separately generated estimates and were not treated as exact reciprocals.[399][400]

Fanelli et al. (5 Jul 2026)
